title: The End Justifies the Mean: A Linear Ranking Rule for Proportional Sequential Decisions
claim: Agreement between a collective choice and an individual preference can be read geometrically as spherical distances and angles, which makes the rule's proportionality properties provable.
layout: 3 panels, left-to-right, sphere then triangle then vector inset, highlighted geodesic
description: Three panels with a shared color code for the points. The left panel shows a unit sphere with the collective vector θ_ang and its antipode −θ_ang in magenta. A green point θ^(i) and a blue point θ′ lie on a great-circle arc labeled G_i. A purple point θ^(j) is joined to θ′ by a geodesic with a yellow highlight, and the angle γ_j sits at −θ_ang. Gray dots mark other voters. A pink plane cuts the sphere at θ_ang. The middle panel redraws the same points as a spherical triangle with sides labeled π − d(θ_ang, θ^(j)), π − d(θ_ang, θ′) and d(θ′, θ^(j)). Its highlighted side carries a > inequality, and γ_j is marked at the angle. The right panel is a pink 2-D box. Gray vectors fan out from θ_ang, with one green and one purple arrow. The eye goes first to the sphere and the yellow highlight.
caption: Geometric interpretation of agreement
abstract: AI alignment and participatory design motivate a new democratic design problem: how to collectively choose a decision rule to use repeatedly. We study this problem for linear ranking rules, which repeatedly rank items $x_j$ within batches $X=(x_1,\dots,x_m)\in(\mathbb{R}^d)^m$, where each item's ranking is dictated by its score $\langle Î¸^*,x_j\rangle$ according to a fixed scoring vector $Î¸^*$. Given voters' preferred scoring vectors $Î¸^{(1)},\dots,Î¸^{(n)}$ and their population fractions $Î±^{(1)},\dots,Î±^{(n)}$, we ask how to choose a collective vector $Î¸^*$ satisfying individual proportionality (IP): every voter type $i$ should agree with the resulting rankings to an $Î±^{(i)}$-proportional degree, either on average over time (long-run IP) or even within each batch (per-batch IP). The default rule, the arithmetic mean of the $Î¸^{(i)}$, has been shown to be severely majoritarian; more generally, it is not clear that any fixed linear rule can balance many voters' disparate opinions. Our main result is that, surprisingly, there is a simple rule that does satisfy long-run IP: the angular mean, the spherical analog of the arithmetic mean. We then show that exact per-batch IP is impossible for fixed linear rules, but that the gap between per-batch and long-run IP shrinks quickly with batch size. Experiments on three real-world preference datasets show that all rules perform similarly when voters' preferences are homogeneous, while the angular mean substantially improves proportionality in high-disagreement regimes.
